reason: Dangerous behaviour shown as heroic: an 11-year-old swims into a rip current to rescue her cousin ('Emma reached the surf first and swam hard') instead of waiting for the lifeguard.
Reads like a health pamphlet: Priya's speech explains the lesson ('she diagnosed an anxiety disorder... It's treatable. I talked to someone and learned ways to cope').
The numbers contradict the tally the plot depends on ('Nine for Dev, eight for Luca... Dev's winning sixty percent... Luca's at fifty-three'), and Zuri becomes 'Ziri'.
The plot loses track of itself: after they are home ('as they turned onto their street') he 'ran back inside the store... and caught up with his mom at the register'.
Confused math logic a grade 6 reader cannot follow ('aim it like a plotted point'), and it ends with reaching into the machine ('reached through the prize flap, and nudged the ball') shown as clever.
Misused hard words and a tacked-on lecture: 'Spontaneous combustion in the engine... the motive power' and 'Kind of like ants colonizing a whole picnic because one crumb fell'.
Dialogue contradicts the scene, making the cause-and-effect confusing: 'Mine stayed up top because I only ever gave them a little drink. Yours went down hunting for water.'
Muddled who-wronged-whom, with the lesson given as a definition: 'Forgiving just means letting go of resentment. Reconciling means rebuilding the relationship.'
The plot loses its own test: 'Priya leaned over the small bowl, sniffed it, and frowned. "Declan. Why is your roast all sweet?"' comes after a Maillard explanation that reads like a textbook.
Forced, confusing required words: 'Four goals to two, which Mateo would notice was the equivalent of a two-goal lead the whole second half.'
Incoherent test and a digression: 'Her percentages moved the same way when she combined groups, which meant the thing on the baseball site wasn't a typo.'
The plot contradicts itself: with the left wrist in a cast she plans to 'make my left hand do things on purpose', and 'Last time was an anomaly' is misused.

Ending contradicts itself: Marcus reads 'his old sheet' and says 'You only lost by two points because you skipped the dog last year', which loses track of who won and why; 'refract' is also used wrongly.
The central event contradicts itself: she spells 'P I N N A C...' and then says 'she had already said one N, and only one'.
Plot loses its thread: the bet is to prove no .400 hitter since 1941, but his honor-roll survey proves nothing about it, yet the grandfather pays anyway.
Plot loses track: the little brother in the car becomes 'Theo', who was introduced as the absent cousin ('Wait,' Theo said slowly).
Broken forced word: 'Rebecca had appoint... no, she had been told to report here', and the story stops on a question.
Reasoning reads too young for grade 7: the whole discovery is 'So wet paint washes out, and dry paint just... stays.'
Plot loses track: Jaxon answers his own worry ('That's what I thought too,' Jaxon said) and 'The kid' appears without being introduced.
Plot loses track of itself: Mya has 'five dollars in her pocket' but pays 'Twelve dollars even', and 'In the window's reflection, the store's weekly revenue probably came from...' is nonsensical.
Plot drifts from the cast to an unrelated paper-airplane contest and stops mid-scene on 'Try it backwards', after a Mathijsen info-dump.
Garbled word '欺骗ing defenders' and a contradiction: a 13-year-old 7th grader recalls 'his own eighth-grade soccer tryout' last year.
Plot loses track of its own timeline: the party is Friday, yet 'He proposed moving the taco bar from Wednesday to Friday'.
Muddled plot (teacher's question, then 'I handed out two versions') and forced aside 'the word extinction ran through her head'.
Plot loses track of itself: Marcus answers 'You're gonna look in the drawer' when the treasure was under the fork, yet Tyler says 'He passed', and the census/recount aside is forced.
Plot loses track: 'found them all empty too' yet the pills were 'put back wherever he liked', and the 'fourth-grader's invention' line is confusing.
Muddled opening: 'his mom was already laughing about it, so the two of them sat on the translucent glass porch table', then Tyler is suddenly the one present.
Plot contradicts itself: the cat 'was locked in the basement all afternoon' yet was also 'asleep', and Marcus 'didn't want to be blamed for leaving the basement door open'.
Reads younger than grade 8 ('half the fifth grade had gathered' at the monkey bars), and she mocks an injured classmate: 'did her best not to smile'.
Result contradicts the fix: after moving the runoff away, 'The cup on the ledge held half an inch of water' and the floor is dry, so the test does not add up.

Plot reasoning contradicts itself: Priya is slower in the short pool, yet the story's fix ('fewer turns meant you couldn't push off') and 'Her tryout time just couldn't be stacked against summer races' would predict the opposite, leaving the resolution confusing.
Ending loses track of its own events: Madison cropped out and never posted her address, yet Deshawn's post gets the comment 'Nice house on 314 Elmont, by the way.'
Plot contradicts itself: the party is a surprise for Priya, yet Kate calls Priya to explain the Bcc plan and Priya says 'So you can invite the class without sharing everyone's email.'

Muddled reasoning and info-dump: minus-lens Sadie concludes 'So near stuff is blurry for me, far stuff is blurry for you', inverting the story's own logic, plus Priya's retina lecture and misused 'optometter'.

The answer is overheard and then recited three times like a drill ('on Vaisakhi, in 1699, Guru Gobind Singh... founded the Khalsa at Anandpur'), and the required word is forced into nonsense ('migratory birds painted... labeled with routes people had walked').

The key deduction does not follow ('The donation box. A square box, big enough to hold twelve cans'), and the thief is won over by a plaque ('Started in 1967... One man. Huh.'), so a grade-8 reader cannot follow the reasoning.
